metadata.title: Efficient Computation of Positional Population Counts Using SIMD Instructions

extraction_notes.note: No theorem-style environments: every node is prose. The C++/AVX-512 implementations (CSA, CSA_AVX512, scalar baseline, 256 B and 1 kB circuits, counter increment) are code listings in figures; only their prose descriptions became algorithm nodes.
problem or definition: the paper names pospopcnt an 'operation', but it is the computational task the algorithms solve, so typed problem.
Instruction-count analysis is a chain of arithmetic estimates in prose; each stated count became a claim, linked in order.
Performance tables (Table 3), the branch-prediction remark and the 'expect fewer instructions per word' aside were left out as data/discussion.
The 256 B circuit walk-through says 'the first 512 B of inputs' and produces B3, which belongs to the 512 B circuit; copied verbatim.

nodes.name: Population count
nodes.statement: In many applications such as deep learning\cite{Dai2017,Courbariaux2016,Zhang2018,Hubara2016}, indexing\cite{Lemire2016}, chemistry\cite{Haque2011}, cryptography\cite{Sanyal2018}, and bioinformatics\cite{Layer2016,Danek2018,Wu2010,Purcell2007} it is desirable to compute the number of set bits in a computer word. This operation is referred to as the population count (\texttt{popcnt}), Hamming weight, or the sideways sum of the word.
differentia: compute the number of set bits in a computer word
nodes.statement_short: The population count (popcnt, Hamming weight, sideways sum) is the number of set bits in a word.

nodes.name: One-hot encoding
nodes.statement: It is common to represent categorical variables using one-hot (1-of-$k$) encoding\cite{lippert2013exhaustive,mittag2015influence} where each categorical value maps to a corresponding bit within a $k$-bit word and each word may only have a single bit set.
differentia: each categorical value maps to a corresponding bit within a $k$-bit word
each word may only have a single bit set

nodes.name: Frequency histogram
nodes.statement: In this context, we want to compute the frequency histogram, that is the number of occurrences of each value.
differentia: the number of occurrences of each value

nodes.name: Positional population count (pospopcnt)
nodes.statement: We name this novel generalization of the population count operation to individual bits spanning multiple words as the \textit{positional population count} (\texttt{pospopcnt}). If each word is made of $k$-bits then we want to compute $k$~counts representing the total number of set bits at each of the $k$~positions.
also_stated_at: Given a stream of $k$-bit words, we seek to compute $k$~distinct sums corresponding to bit values at indexes 0, 1, 2, \ldots, $k-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Given a stream of $k$-bit words, compute the $k$ counts of set bits at each bit position across all words.

nodes.name: Positional popcount speedup over scalar baseline
nodes.statement: Notably, we show that our proposed algorithm can be in excess of 50-fold faster compared to a baseline scalar approach, as long as the input is sufficiently large (several kilobytes).
assumptions: as long as the input is sufficiently large (several kilobytes)
conclusions: our proposed algorithm can be in excess of 50-fold faster compared to a baseline scalar approach

nodes.name: Wilkes-Wheeler-Gill population count
nodes.statement: One of the earliest efficient algorithm to compute the population count is the Wilkes-Wheeler-Gill population-count\cite{Wilkes} (Fig.~\ref{fig:tree-of-adders}). This algorithm begins by adding adjacent bits into two-bit subwords, then adds these two-bit subwords into four-bit subwords, and finally adds adjacent four-bit subwords into byte values. These byte values are then summed using a multiplication and a bit-shift.
nodes.statement_short: Tree of adders: sum adjacent bits into 2-bit, then 4-bit, then byte subwords, then sum bytes with a multiply and shift.

nodes.name: Harley-Seal algorithm
nodes.statement: Another efficient approach\cite{warren2007} is the Harley-Seal algorithm that is based on carry-save adder (CSA) networks frequently used in hardware microarchitectures.

nodes.name: Carry-save adder (CSA) subroutine
nodes.statement: The CSA subroutine takes three input words and produce two output words: (1) a sequence of partial sum bits, and (2) a sequence of carry bits.
differentia: takes three input words and produce two output words
a sequence of partial sum bits

nodes.name: Bitwise formula for a three-bit sum
nodes.statement: Given three~bit values ($a,b,c\in \{0,1\}$), the sum $a + b + c$ is computed as a 2-bit word where the least significant bit is given by $(a\mathrm{xor} b) \mathrm{xor} c$ and the most significant bit is given by $(a \mathrm{bitand} b) \mathrm{bitor} ( (a \mathrm{xor} b) \mathrm{bitand} c )$.
conclusions: the least significant bit is given by $(a\mathrm{xor} b) \mathrm{xor} c$
the most significant bit is given by $(a \mathrm{bitand} b) \mathrm{bitor} ( (a \mathrm{xor} b) \mathrm{bitand} c )$
nodes.statement_short: The 2-bit sum of three bits has LSB $a\oplus b\oplus c$ and MSB $ab \lor ((a\oplus b)c)$.

nodes.name: Proof that three bits sum in five operations
nodes.statement: We reuse the $a \mathrm{xor} b$ expression from the computation of the least significant bit when computing the most significant bit.
nodes.statement_short: Share the common subexpression $a\oplus b$ between the LSB and MSB formulas.

nodes.name: Three values summed with five logical operations
nodes.statement: Therefore, three values can be summed using 5~logical operations.
also_stated_at: The conventional approach for computing the CSA routine requires 5~logical operations.
conclusions: three values can be summed using 5~logical operations

nodes.name: Four-input CSA circuit (Harley-Seal)
nodes.statement: Let us illustrate this approach by computing the population count of four inputs words using a simplified circuit (Fig.~\ref{fig:hsillustration}). Starting with two 64-bit words initialized to zero: one for the least significant bits ($B_0$) and one for the second least significant bits ($B_1$). \begin{enumerate} \item Two input words are summed with $B_0$ using a CSA subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}) resulting in two outputs: one corresponding to the least significant bits stored in $B_0$ and another corresponding to the second most significant bit: let us call it $x$. \item Two new input words are summed with $B_0$ using the same CSA subroutine. Again the output corresponding to the least significant bit is stored in $B_0$. We have a second output corresponding to the second most significant bits, let us call it $y$. \item In the final step, $x$, $y$, and $B_1$ are added together. The output corresponding to the least significant bits is stored in $B_1$. Similarly, the output corresponding to the most significant bit is stored in $B_2$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Sum four input words with three CSA calls, keeping running bit-planes $B_0$, $B_1$ and producing $B_2$.

nodes.name: Population count from CSA bit-planes
nodes.statement: If $c_i$ is the population count of $B_i$, then the population count of the four words is $1 c_0 + 2 c_1 + 4 c_2$.
conclusions: the population count of the four words is $1 c_0 + 2 c_1 + 4 c_2$

nodes.name: CSA circuit on $2^N$ words
nodes.statement: In general, given $2^N$~input words, we can produce $N+1$~words corresponding to the sum of the bits using a CSA circuit. Then the per-word population count can be computed from the resulting $N$~words.
conclusions: we can produce $N+1$~words corresponding to the sum of the bits using a CSA circuit
the per-word population count can be computed from the resulting $N$~words

nodes.name: Recursive construction of CSA circuits
nodes.statement: Assume that we have a circuit that takes $2^N$~inputs as well as $B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1}$ and produces the updated $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$ corresponding to the sum. We can represent this circuit as a function $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$ that outputs $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$. We can then construct a larger circuit that takes twice as many inputs by two calls to the circuit together with an additional CSA routine. Indeed, to compute $F_{N+1} (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N})$, we can start by computing $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$. We provide the first $N$~outputs ($B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$) from this first call to $F_N$ to a second call to the circuit $F_N$, this time using the $2^N$ following inputs $d_N, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}$. We are left with three values $B_N$, one was provided as an input to $F_{N+1}$, and two have been produced by a call to the smaller circuit $F_N$. We can combine these with a CSA routine.
nodes.statement_short: Recursion: build $F_{N+1}$ from two calls to $F_N$ plus one CSA combining the three $B_N$ values.

nodes.name: $2^N-1$ CSA routines suffice for $2^N$ inputs
nodes.statement: By such a recursive argument, we can show that $2^N-1$~CSA routines is sufficient to process $2^N$~inputs.
conclusions: $2^N-1$~CSA routines is sufficient to process $2^N$~inputs

nodes.name: SIMD CSA network is the fastest population count
nodes.statement: Given sufficiently large input arrays (e.g., 1\,kB), such a SIMD-accelerated CSA network is superior to all known population count alternatives on current Intel processors\cite{mula2017faster}.
conclusions: such a SIMD-accelerated CSA network is superior to all known population count alternatives on current Intel processors

nodes.name: CSA in two AVX-512 instructions
nodes.statement: On processors with the AVX-512 instruction set architecture available, we can simplify this subroutine down to two instructions by using the three-operand instruction \texttt{vpternlogd} using the \texttt{\_mm512\_ternarylogic\_epi32} intrinsic function (Fig.~\ref{fig:csa-avx512}).
assumptions: On processors with the AVX-512 instruction set architecture available
conclusions: we can simplify this subroutine down to two instructions by using the three-operand instruction \texttt{vpternlogd}

nodes.name: vpternlogd instruction
nodes.statement: The \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction operates on three input bits $a$, $b$, $c$ and an 8-bit sequence $i$ and returns the bit at index $1a + 2b + 4c$ of $i$.
differentia: operates on three input bits $a$, $b$, $c$ and an 8-bit sequence $i$
returns the bit at index $1a + 2b + 4c$ of $i$

nodes.name: vpternlogd computes any ternary Boolean function
nodes.statement: The \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction can compute any ternary Boolean function using a single instruction.
conclusions: The \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction can compute any ternary Boolean function using a single instruction

nodes.name: Derivation of vpternlogd immediates 150 and 232
nodes.statement: This instruction is useful in computing the most and least significant bits in the CSA routine. To determine the value of the 8-bit sequence $i$ in the context of computing the least and most significant bits, it suffices to enumerate all 8~possible inputs (Table~\ref{tab:csatern}). \begin{itemize} \item The least significant bit can be computed as the \texttt{xor} of the three inputs. Therefore, the \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction computes the desired output when the bits at index $\{1, 2, 4, 7\}$ of $i$ are set. In software, this bit sequence is represented as the integer 0b10010110 in binary or 150 in decimal. \item Computing the most significant bits involves the expression $(a \mathrm{~and~} b) \mathrm{~or~} ((a \mathrm{~xor~} b) \mathrm{~and~} c$. We can achieve this result by setting the bits at index \{3, 5, 6, 7\} of $i$ that can be represented as the binary string 0b11101000 or 232 in decimal.
nodes.statement_short: Enumerate the 8 inputs (truth table) to read off the immediates: 150 for xor (LSB), 232 for majority (MSB).

nodes.name: AVX-512 CSA gain factor of 20
nodes.statement: When comparing the resulting AVX-512 routine to its 64-bit equivalent (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}), we observe that the AVX-512-based CSA subroutine can process 8~times as many bits (512 versus 64) while simultaneously reducing the number of logical operations from 5 to 2. Taken together, we achieve a gain factor of $5/2 \times 8 = 20$ in terms of instructions per input bits.
conclusions: the AVX-512-based CSA subroutine can process 8~times as many bits (512 versus 64) while simultaneously reducing the number of logical operations from 5 to 2
we achieve a gain factor of $5/2 \times 8 = 20$ in terms of instructions per input bits

nodes.name: Restriction to 16-bit words
nodes.statement: Wider words (larger universes) can be encoded into multiple distinct streams of 16-bit words. In addition, our algorithms can be generalized to wider words without difficulty.

nodes.name: Scalar shift-mask-add positional population count
nodes.statement: To compute the positional population count, we start with sixteen zero-initialized bit-counters. Next, we iterate over the bits in each word in sequence while incrementing the corresponding target bit-counter as needed. A sensible baseline algorithm for computing the positional population count involves a shift-mask-add subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-naive}): \begin{enumerate} \item Right shift a 16-bit word by the bit index $p\in\{ 0,1,\ldots,15\}$. Mathematically, this is equivalent to an integer division by $2^p$ with the result being the integer quotient. \item Mask out all but the least significant bit from the shifted word. This bit is set when the quotient is odd, and zero otherwise. \item Increment the counter at position $p$ with the value from step 2. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: for each 16-bit word and each bit index $p$, shift right by $p$, mask the LSB, and add it to counter $p$.

nodes.name: Scalar baseline cost estimate
nodes.statement: For sufficiently long input streams, we estimate the number of executed instructions to $\sim$4 per bit for a total of $\sim$64~instructions per 16-bit word. Given that most recent Intel processors can retire four instructions per CPU cycle, we expect a processing speed of around 16~cycles per 16-bit word for this scalar shift-mask-add subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-naive}).
assumptions: most recent Intel processors can retire four instructions per CPU cycle
conclusions: the number of executed instructions to $\sim$4 per bit for a total of $\sim$64~instructions per 16-bit word
a processing speed of around 16~cycles per 16-bit word for this scalar shift-mask-add subroutine

nodes.name: CSA_AVX512 calls per circuit size
nodes.statement: The simplest network (Fig.~\ref{fig:hsillustration}) takes four 512-bit registers (or 256\,B) as inputs (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512-small}) and uses three calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function. We can double the size of the network and process 512\,B inputs using seven calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function. Again, doubling the network size, we can process 1\,kB inputs using fifteen calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512}).
conclusions: takes four 512-bit registers (or 256\,B) as inputs (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512-small}) and uses three calls
process 512\,B inputs using seven calls
process 1\,kB inputs using fifteen calls

nodes.name: Two instructions per CSA_AVX512 call
nodes.statement: Each call to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function involves only two instructions (two times \texttt{vpternlogd}).
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the number of CSA calls by the two vpternlogd instructions each call costs.

nodes.name: Circuit instruction counts per block
nodes.statement: Excluding load and store instructions, we use \begin{inparaenum}[(1)] \item 6~instructions per block of 256\,B or \item 14~instructions per block of 512\,B or \item 30~instructions per block of 1\,kB. \end{inparaenum}
conclusions: 6~instructions per block of 256\,B
14~instructions per block of 512\,B
30~instructions per block of 1\,kB.

nodes.name: AVX-512 CSA positional population count
nodes.statement: At the end of each circuit, we have a set of registers \{\texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}, \ldots\} corresponding, for each bit position in $i\in [0,1,\ldots, 512)$, to the sum of set bits. For simplicity let us assume that we are working with the smaller circuit (256\,B). Before starting the procedure, the registers \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} and the 16 output bit-counters are zero-initialized. Next, the first 512\,B of inputs are process with the circuit and receive as output the updated values of \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. In addition, we also receive a new register \texttt{B3} corresponding to the fourth least significant bit of the sum of the set bits at position $i\in [0,1,\ldots, 512)$. We can update our sixteen bit-counters by checking the bits in \texttt{B3}: the first counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{0, 16, 32, \ldots, 496\}$, the second counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{1, 17, 33, \ldots, 497\}$, and so forth. The process of loading the next 512\,B of input data, call the circuit, and providing it with the updated values \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} is repeated until no more data is available. At this point, when no more input data is available, we must increment our bit-counters with the remaining bits in \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. These are processed as \texttt{B3} except that the multiplier is 1, 2 and 4 respectively. The algorithms using the large circuits (512\,B and 1\,kB) work similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Feed blocks through a CSA circuit with running bit-plane registers; add the overflow plane B3 (weight 8) to the 16 counters, then flush B0-B2 with weights 1, 2, 4.

nodes.name: Vectorized counter increment
nodes.statement: The inner loop of our algorithm, where the bit-counters from the \texttt{B3} register are updated could become expensive. This loop execute 16~sums of 32~bit values and multiply the result by eight. This final multiplication can be deferred until the end of the main loop. Further, we vectorize the sum (Fig.~\ref{fig:increment-avx512}) by using sixteen vector of counters, each spanning 512~bits, or thirty-two 16-bit counters, instead of using sixteen scalar counters. Given the \texttt{B3} register, we select the least significant bit of each 16-bit word by using a mask-select operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_and_si512} intrinsic function. Next, we increment counters using a horizontal add operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_add_epi16} intrinsic. Finally, we shift each 16-bit subword of the \texttt{B3} register right by one bit with the \texttt{_mm512_srli_epi16} intrinsic function. This procedure can be written in scalar form as:\\ \begin{cpp}[0.8\columnwidth] for (pos = 0; pos < 16; ++pos) { for (i = 0; i < 32; ++i) { counter[pos] += B[i] & 1; B[i] >>= 1; } } \end{cpp} \\ with the convention that the subword $B$ at index $i$ (\texttt{B[i]}) selects a 16-bit word within \texttt{B}.
nodes.statement_short: Update 16 vector counters from B3 by repeated mask-LSB, 16-bit add, and shift-right-by-one; defer the multiply by 8.

nodes.name: 48 instructions for the counter update
nodes.statement: By unrolling this vectorized code, we achieve $3 \times 16=48$~instructions, without considering overhead and load/store instructions.
conclusions: $3 \times 16=48$~instructions

nodes.name: Total instructions per block
nodes.statement: We can add these 48~instructions to our previous counts: \begin{inparaenum}[(1)] \item 54 instructions per block of 256\,B or \item 62 instructions per block of 512\,B or \item 78~instructions per block of 1\,kB. \end{inparaenum}
conclusions: 54 instructions per block of 256\,B
62 instructions per block of 512\,B
78~instructions per block of 1\,kB.

nodes.name: Instructions per 16-bit word
nodes.statement: Dividing by the number of 16-bit words processed, we get the following instruction counts per word: \begin{enumerate} \item 0.42 when using blocks of 256\,B, \item 0.24 when using blocks of 512\,B, and \item 0.15 when using blocks of 1\,kB. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: 0.42 when using blocks of 256\,B
0.24 when using blocks of 512\,B
0.15 when using blocks of  1\,kB.

nodes.name: Over 400-fold instruction reduction
nodes.statement: In comparison, we estimate about 64~instructions per 16-bit word for the scalar version. This corresponds to a $>$400-fold reduction in the number of executed instructions.
conclusions: a $>$400-fold reduction in the number of executed instructions

nodes.name: Overhead of recovering counts
nodes.statement: This analysis ignores the overhead cost of recovering the counts from both the vectorized counters and the running registers $\{\texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}, \ldots\}$. For small inputs, this overhead can occupy a dominant proportion of the total cost. For example, the sixteen vector counters span 1\,kB on their own. Hence, to achieve good performance, the input stream should at least exceed 1\,kB.
nodes.statement_short: The analysis ignores a fixed ~1 kB counter-recovery overhead, so inputs should exceed 1 kB.

nodes.name: Summary of SIMD CSA networks and residual handling
nodes.statement: Taken together, we describe several SIMD-accelerated CSA networks of different sizes for computing the positional population count with up to $>$400-fold reduction in the number of executed instructions compared to a scalar implementation. Our SIMD-based approach can compute the positional population count for inputs that are a multiple of 256\,B. Any residual input values will be processed using a scalar subroutine.

nodes.name: Performance independent of input data
nodes.statement: However, we find that performance is independent of the input data as our algorithms do not branch on the content of the data.
conclusions: performance is independent of the input data

nodes.name: Fixed overhead dominates tiny inputs
nodes.statement: Our proposed AVX-512-based approach has a fixed overhead, irrespective of the input stream size. This overhead is non-negligible for small inputs. For tiny inputs (512~words), we need about 30~instructions per 16-bit word, and almost all of these instructions are part of the overhead. However, once we reach a few thousands words (e.g., 4096~words or 8\,kB), our AVX-512-based approach becomes beneficial.

nodes.name: Scalar algorithm has fixed speed
nodes.statement: For the scalar algorithm, we observe a fixed speed over the range of inputs in our experiments: 17~cycles and 65~instructions per input word.

nodes.name: 1 kB-block AVX-512 algorithm is fastest
nodes.statement: Overall, the fastest approach is our proposed AVX-512 algorithm with large block size (1\,kB), except maybe for inputs of less than 64\,kB.

nodes.name: Scaling with input size
nodes.statement: Increasing the input size reduce the number of instructions per input word and simultaneously increase speed. Due to diminishing returns, the performance for 1\,GB inputs are practically identical to that of 256\,MB.

nodes.name: 300-fold fewer instructions than scalar
nodes.statement: In the best scenario, the AVX-512 approach uses 300~times fewer instructions compared to the scalar approach.

nodes.name: Speed close to memcpy
nodes.statement: As a reference point, the C \texttt{memcpy} function runs at a speed of 20\,GB/s for large inputs compared to 18 GB/s for the positional popcount operation on large inputs.

nodes.name: Near memory-copy speed with AVX-512
nodes.statement: We demonstrate that we can process 16-bit words at nearly the speed of a memory copy when AVX-512 is available and when the input size is sufficiently large (e.g., 256\,MB).
assumptions: when the input size is sufficiently large (e.g., 256\,MB)
conclusions: we can process 16-bit words at nearly the speed of a memory copy

nodes.name: Best algorithm over 40 times faster
nodes.statement: Our best algorithm is over 40~times faster compared to a non-vectorized approach.

nodes.name: Pair bits
nodes.statement: adding adjacent bits into two-bit subwords

nodes.name: Pair 2-bit subwords
nodes.statement: adds these two-bit subwords into four-bit subwords

nodes.name: Form byte values
nodes.statement: adds adjacent four-bit subwords into byte values

nodes.name: Sum bytes
nodes.statement: These byte values are then summed using a multiplication and a bit-shift.

nodes.name: Zero bit-planes
nodes.statement: Starting with two 64-bit words initialized to zero: one for the least significant bits ($B_0$) and one for the second least significant bits ($B_1$).

nodes.name: First CSA
nodes.statement: Two input words are summed with $B_0$ using a CSA subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}) resulting in two outputs: one corresponding to the least significant bits stored in $B_0$ and another corresponding to the second most significant bit: let us call it $x$.

nodes.name: Second CSA
nodes.statement: Two new input words are summed with $B_0$ using the same CSA subroutine. Again the output corresponding to the least significant bit is stored in $B_0$. We have a second output corresponding to the second most significant bits, let us call it $y$.

nodes.name: Combine carries
nodes.statement: In the final step, $x$, $y$, and $B_1$ are added together. The output corresponding to the least significant bits is stored in $B_1$. Similarly, the output corresponding to the most significant bit is stored in $B_2$.

nodes.name: Assume $F_N$
nodes.statement: Assume that we have a circuit that takes $2^N$~inputs as well as $B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1}$ and produces the updated $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$ corresponding to the sum. We can represent this circuit as a function $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$ that outputs $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a circuit $F_N$ summing $2^N$ inputs into bit-planes.

nodes.name: Doubling plan
nodes.statement: We can then construct a larger circuit that takes twice as many inputs by two calls to the circuit together with an additional CSA routine.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: two calls to $F_N$ plus one CSA give $F_{N+1}$.

nodes.name: Two calls to $F_N$
nodes.statement: Indeed, to compute $F_{N+1} (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N})$, we can start by computing $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$. We provide the first $N$~outputs ($B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$) from this first call to $F_N$ to a second call to the circuit $F_N$, this time using the $2^N$ following inputs $d_N, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Run $F_N$ on the first half, then again on the second half with the updated planes.

nodes.name: Combine with CSA
nodes.statement: We are left with three values $B_N$, one was provided as an input to $F_{N+1}$, and two have been produced by a call to the smaller circuit $F_N$. We can combine these with a CSA routine.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the three resulting $B_N$ values with one CSA.

nodes.name: Enumerate inputs
nodes.statement: This instruction is useful in computing the most and least significant bits in the CSA routine. To determine the value of the 8-bit sequence $i$ in the context of computing the least and most significant bits, it suffices to enumerate all 8~possible inputs (Table~\ref{tab:csatern}).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to enumerating the 8 input combinations.

nodes.name: LSB immediate
nodes.statement: The least significant bit can be computed as the \texttt{xor} of the three inputs. Therefore, the \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction computes the desired output when the bits at index $\{1, 2, 4, 7\}$ of $i$ are set. In software, this bit sequence is represented as the integer 0b10010110 in binary or 150 in decimal.
nodes.statement_short: LSB is xor: immediate 0b10010110 = 150.

nodes.name: MSB immediate
nodes.statement: Computing the most significant bits involves the expression $(a \mathrm{~and~} b) \mathrm{~or~} ((a \mathrm{~xor~} b) \mathrm{~and~} c$. We can achieve this result by setting the bits at index \{3, 5, 6, 7\} of $i$ that can be represented as the binary string 0b11101000 or 232 in decimal.
nodes.statement_short: MSB is majority: immediate 0b11101000 = 232.

nodes.name: Zero counters
nodes.statement: To compute the positional population count, we start with sixteen zero-initialized bit-counters.

nodes.name: Iterate bits
nodes.statement: Next, we iterate over the bits in each word in sequence while incrementing the corresponding target bit-counter as needed.

nodes.name: Shift
nodes.statement: Right shift a 16-bit word by the bit index $p\in\{ 0,1,\ldots,15\}$. Mathematically, this is equivalent to an integer division by $2^p$ with the result being the integer quotient.

nodes.name: Mask
nodes.statement: Mask out all but the least significant bit from the shifted word. This bit is set when the quotient is odd, and zero otherwise.

nodes.name: Increment
nodes.statement: Increment the counter at position $p$ with the value from step 2.

nodes.name: Zero registers
nodes.statement: Before starting the procedure, the registers \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} and the 16 output bit-counters are zero-initialized.

nodes.name: Run circuit
nodes.statement: Next, the first 512\,B of inputs are process with the circuit and receive as output the updated values of \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. In addition, we also receive a new register \texttt{B3} corresponding to the fourth least significant bit of the sum of the set bits at position $i\in [0,1,\ldots, 512)$.
nodes.statement_short: Run a block through the CSA circuit, updating B0-B2 and producing B3.

nodes.name: Add B3 to counters
nodes.statement: We can update our sixteen bit-counters by checking the bits in \texttt{B3}: the first counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{0, 16, 32, \ldots, 496\}$, the second counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{1, 17, 33, \ldots, 497\}$, and so forth.
nodes.statement_short: Add 8 times the per-position bit counts of B3 to the 16 counters.

nodes.name: Repeat over blocks
nodes.statement: The process of loading the next 512\,B of input data, call the circuit, and providing it with the updated values \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} is repeated until no more data is available.

nodes.name: Flush B0-B2
nodes.statement: At this point, when no more input data is available, we must increment our bit-counters with the remaining bits in \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. These are processed as \texttt{B3} except that the multiplier is 1, 2 and 4 respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Add the remaining bits of B0, B1, B2 with weights 1, 2, 4.

nodes.name: Defer multiply
nodes.statement: This final multiplication can be deferred until the end of the main loop.

nodes.name: Vector counters
nodes.statement: Further, we vectorize the sum (Fig.~\ref{fig:increment-avx512}) by using sixteen vector of counters, each spanning 512~bits, or thirty-two 16-bit counters, instead of using sixteen scalar counters.

nodes.name: Mask LSB
nodes.statement: Given the \texttt{B3} register, we select the least significant bit of each 16-bit word by using a mask-select operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_and_si512} intrinsic function.

nodes.name: Add
nodes.statement: Next, we increment counters using a horizontal add operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_add_epi16} intrinsic.

nodes.name: Shift
nodes.statement: Finally, we shift each 16-bit subword of the \texttt{B3} register right by one bit with the \texttt{_mm512_srli_epi16} intrinsic function.
